Note to Dhruv's parents, Class 4
Today in creative writing, Dhruv wrote a story about a grandmother who 'walks with a stick and forgets the kettle on'. He added, 'The boy is scared she will fall and die.' At break he asked me quietly whether old people's legs stop working. I think he is worried about his Dadi. I told him simply that as people get older their bodies slow down and sometimes need more help, and that it's normal to feel scared and to love them at the same time. He seemed relieved to talk. You might find a shared job he can do with Dadi, like watering plants or reading together, so he feels close rather than frightened. Happy to talk more.
Rukmini, class teacher

subtype: Young person meeting a grandparent's forgetfulness [Observer]
passage: Ira, nineteen, had agreed to stay with Nana Jagdish for one evening while her parents went to a wedding. Then the power went out. In the dark, Nana got up and started walking towards the front door. 'I have to go to the office. They'll be waiting.' He had retired twenty years ago. 'Nana, there's no office. Sit down!' she said, too sharply. He turned, confused and frightened. 'Who are you? Where's my Kamla?' Ira's throat tightened. Nani had died years ago. She took a breath and remembered what her mother had said: it's the illness, not him. She lit a candle and spoke softly. 'Nana, it's Ira. It's night now. The office is closed. Shall we have tea?' He looked at her for a long time, then sat. 'Tea would be nice.' She held his hand until the lights came back.

qa.q: What did Ira light when the power went out?
qa.a: A candle.

qa.q: What did Ira feel when Nana asked for Kamla?
qa.a: She felt a tightening grief, since Nani had died years ago, and fear at his confusion.

qa.q: What helped Ira respond gently instead of sharply?
qa.a: Remembering it was the illness, not him, then speaking softly and redirecting him to tea.

qa.q: How might Nana have felt when Ira spoke sharply?
qa.a: He probably felt confused and frightened, not knowing who she was or why she was cross.

grounding: Shows a young person facing a grandparent's confusion with impatience and grief, and learning that it is illness so she can respond gently.

subtopic: Dementia in a relative
passage:
'Dadu, it's Tanuja. Your granddaughter.'
Arnab looked at her face for a long moment. 'I know. I know that.' His hands twisted the edge of his shawl. 'I just… I lost the word.'
'It's okay.'
'It isn't okay.' His voice rose. 'I went to the kitchen three times today and forgot why. Your Dida's photo is on the wall and I couldn't remember her name. Do you know how that feels?'
Tanuja sat beside him. 'It sounds frightening.'
'It is.' His anger crumbled. 'And I'm embarrassed. I used to teach mathematics. Now I can't find the bathroom.'
'You're still my Dadu. You taught me my tables.'
He smiled faintly. 'Seven sevens?'
'Forty-nine.'
'Good girl.' He patted her hand. 'At least I haven't forgotten that.'

qa.q: What subject did Arnab use to teach?
qa.a: Mathematics.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling as he talked about forgetting?
qa.a: He felt frightened, angry and embarrassed, aware that something was wrong with his memory.

qa.q: What did Tanuja do that kept Arnab's dignity?
qa.a: She listened, named his fear, reminded him who he still was and joined him in the times-tables game.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt hearing Dadu forget Dida's name?
qa.a: She was probably sad and shaken, but chose to stay calm and warm for him.

grounding: Shows a person living with memory loss feeling frightened, angry and embarrassed yet still loving, and a granddaughter treating him as a whole person.

subtopic: Dementia in a relative
passage: My name is Gurpreet, and I know something is wrong with me. Last month I got lost driving to my own daughter Charu's house, a route I've driven a hundred times. I sat in the car outside a strange temple and cried, and I haven't cried since my wife died. Charu calls me Papa and hugs me, but sometimes I can see the worry in her eyes when I ask the same thing twice. The doctor has a word for it now. I don't like the word. I hate the way people start speaking slowly to me, as if I'm a child. I still love my granddaughter's drawings. I still feel embarrassed when I spill my tea. I'm still me in here, even when I can't find the door. I just want them to remember that.

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet get lost driving to?
qa.a: Charu's house.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet feel when people speak slowly to him?
qa.a: He feels hurt and belittled, as if being treated like a child.

qa.q: What would help Gurpreet feel respected?
qa.a: Being spoken to normally and treated as the same person, with feelings and dignity, even when he forgets.

qa.q: How might Charu feel when Gurpreet asks the same thing twice?
qa.a: She probably feels worried and sad, seeing her father change.

grounding: Shows a person living with memory loss who is frightened and aware something is wrong, yet still feels love, embarrassment and dignity and wants to be treated as himself.

subtopic: Dementia in a relative
passage:
Day centre note, Thursday
Nirmala, who lives with dementia, arrived upset this morning. She kept asking where her handbag was and accused another member of taking it. When I tried to guide her to a chair, she pushed my hand away and shouted, 'Don't treat me like a baby!' I stepped back and spoke to her as I would any adult. 'You're right, I'm sorry. Let's look for it together.' We found it under her chair. She looked embarrassed. 'I'm getting so stupid.' I told her she wasn't stupid, and that losing things is part of the illness, not her fault. Later she showed me a photo of her granddaughter on her phone and glowed as she told me about her. She laughed at the singing session. Please let her family know she had a good afternoon.
Avni, day centre carer

qa.q: Where did Avni and Nirmala find the handbag?
qa.a: Under her chair.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when she said she was getting stupid?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and ashamed after accusing someone and finding the bag herself.

qa.q: What did Avni do that protected Nirmala's dignity?
qa.a: Avni apologised, spoke to her as an adult, searched with her and reassured her it was the illness, not her fault.

qa.q: How might the member Nirmala accused have felt?
qa.a: That person may have felt hurt or shocked at being accused, even if they understood it was the illness.

grounding: Shows a person with dementia feeling frightened, angry and embarrassed yet still loving and proud, and a carer treating her with dignity as a person.

subtopic: Dementia in a relative
passage: It was Eid, and Rashmi, twenty-five, had cooked all night, because Ammi had always made the sheer khurma and now she couldn't. Relatives were arriving at noon. At eleven, Ammi came into the kitchen, looked at Rashmi and asked politely, 'Are you the new cook?' Rashmi gripped the counter. The mother who had taught her every recipe was right here, and gone. She felt grief, and then guilt for grieving someone still alive, and pure exhaustion. Her friend Nazia arrived early with extra biryani and found her crying. 'Go sit with her. I'll do the rest.' Rashmi sat with Ammi, who suddenly began humming an old Eid song, and Rashmi joined in, laughing through tears. That night Nazia sent her the details of a carers' support group. 'You shouldn't do this alone.'

qa.q: What did Ammi ask Rashmi in the kitchen?
qa.a: 'Are you the new cook?'

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when Ammi didn't recognise her?
qa.a: She felt grief for a mother still present, guilt for grieving, and exhaustion.

qa.q: What helped Rashmi feel less alone?
qa.a: Nazia taking over the cooking so Rashmi could sit with Ammi, and sending details of a carers' support group.

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt humming the Eid song?
qa.a: She may have felt happy and calm in that moment, connected to an old memory.

grounding: Shows a relative grieving a parent who is changing while still alive, with guilt, exhaustion and moments of joy, and support easing the isolation.

subtopic: Dementia in a relative
passage: In their house in Guwahati, Bhupen, twenty-six, looked after his father while his younger brother Vikas worked in Delhi. Some days Deuta knew him and joked like old times. Other days he called Bhupen by a stranger's name and cried for his own mother. Bhupen felt he was losing his father slowly, a little each week, while still bringing him tea every morning. He felt guilty for sometimes wishing it were over, and too tired to see friends. Then one evening, Deuta suddenly sang an old Bihu song, every word right, and clapped. Bhupen laughed until he cried. That night he called Vikas and told him everything honestly. Vikas promised to come home one week a month. And Bhupen went to his first carers' support group on Saturday. It helped to hear others say what he'd been too ashamed to say.

qa.q: What song did Deuta sing?
qa.a: An old Bihu song.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling as his father changed?
qa.a: He felt a slow grief, guilt for sometimes wishing it were over, and deep tiredness.

qa.q: What steps lessened Bhupen's isolation?
qa.a: Telling Vikas honestly so he would come home monthly, and joining a carers' support group.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel hearing everything from Bhupen?
qa.a: Vikas may feel guilty and sad for not knowing, and glad to help more.

grounding: Shows a relative feeling ambiguous grief, guilt, exhaustion and moments of joy as a parent with dementia changes, and support and honest talk easing isolation.

subtopic: Dementia in a relative
passage:
'Eshaan, how was Ma today?'
'Good morning, bad afternoon. She thought I was Papa. Then she thought I was a thief.'
Vishal sat down heavily. 'I miss her. Isn't that crazy? She's in the next room.'
'It's not crazy. I feel it too. Like she's leaving a bit at a time.'
'And then I feel guilty for missing her while she's right here.'
'Same.' Eshaan rubbed his face. 'I'm so tired, Vishal.'
'I know. You're doing the days. I'm only doing nights.'
'She laughed today, though. At the parrot on the balcony. Really laughed.'
Vishal smiled. 'That's something.'
'The hospital has a support group for families. Thursday evenings.'
'Let's go. Both of us. Neighbour can sit with Ma.'

qa.q: What did Ma laugh at today?
qa.a: The parrot on the balcony.

qa.q: What is Vishal feeling about their mother?
qa.a: He misses her even though she is in the next room, and feels guilty for it.

qa.q: What step do the brothers decide on?
qa.a: Going together to the hospital's family support group on Thursday evenings.

qa.q: How might the neighbour's help affect the brothers?
qa.a: It gives them a short break to get support, so they feel less alone and exhausted.

grounding: Shows relatives grieving a parent who is changing while still alive, with guilt, exhaustion and moments of joy, and a support group and shared care easing isolation.

subtopic: Dementia in a relative
passage:
Tuesday night
Today Dadi asked me 'When is Pooja coming?' at least twenty times. Pooja is my sister. She's coming on Sunday. I answered calmly the first ten times. The eleventh time, I snapped, 'I've told you, Sunday! Sunday!' Dadi's face crumpled and she said sorry. I went to the balcony and felt like the worst grandson on earth.
After that I tried what the doctor's leaflet said. Short, calm answer: 'Sunday, Dadi.' Then change the subject: 'Shall we water the tulsi?' It worked better. She asked again, but she smiled. When my cousin came at six, I went for a twenty-minute walk. I came back with more patience.
I'll forgive myself for the snap. But I'm taking that walk every day.
Darshan

qa.q: When is Pooja coming?
qa.a: On Sunday.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel after snapping at Dadi?
qa.a: Darshan felt guilty and ashamed, like the worst grandson on earth.

qa.q: What strategies helped Darshan keep patience?
qa.a: A short calm answer, gently changing the subject to watering the tulsi, and taking a walk as a break.

qa.q: How might Dadi have felt when Darshan snapped?
qa.a: Dadi probably felt hurt and confused, apologising without understanding why he was upset.

grounding: Shows a caregiver hearing the same question many times, snapping and feeling guilty, and learning brief calm answers, redirection and breaks.

passage:

Vishal: oof. how are you holding up
Anand: badly. I snapped at him. then he looked scared and I felt like a monster

Anand: ok I said 'it's Thursday, Papa' and then asked him to help me sort the old photos. he told me about his army days for an hour

Vishal: I'm coming Saturday. you go out for 2 hours
Anand: thank you. seriously

qa.a: Fifteen times.

qa.q: How did Anand feel after snapping at Papa?
qa.a: Anand felt guilty and awful, like a monster, when Papa looked scared.

subtopic: Dementia in a relative
passage: In their village near Satara, Naveen, twenty-five, had come home from Pune to look after his grandfather. Every few minutes Aba asked, 'Have the buffaloes been fed?' The buffaloes had been sold three years ago. At first Naveen explained every time. Then he found himself shouting, and afterwards he sat behind the cowshed, hating himself. Their neighbour Ayesha, who had cared for her own mother, stopped by with a plate of bhakri. 'Don't argue with it,' she said. 'Just say, yes, Aba, all fed. Then give him something to do.' Naveen tried. 'Yes, Aba, all fed. Come, help me shell groundnuts.' Aba happily shelled groundnuts for an hour. Ayesha also offered to sit with Aba every afternoon so Naveen could walk to the river. The questions didn't stop. But Naveen's kindness came back.

qa.q: What did Aba keep asking about?
qa.a: Whether the buffaloes had been fed.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel after shouting at Aba?
qa.a: He felt guilty and full of self-hatred, sitting behind the cowshed.

qa.q: What approach did Ayesha suggest?
qa.a: A calm brief answer, 'Yes, Aba, all fed', followed by a simple activity, plus afternoon breaks for Naveen.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt helping Naveen?
qa.a: She probably felt understanding and caring, having been through the same with her own mother.

grounding: Shows a caregiver whose patience thins with repeated questions, feeling guilty, and finding brief calm answers, redirection and breaks to keep kindness alive.
